title: Database Fundamentals
summary: A database is a managed collection of data with a query language, integrity rules, and a storage engine.

title: Relational Databases
summary: Data as relations (tables), queried with algebra/calculus, constrained by keys.

title: SQL
summary: The declarative language of relational databases: SELECT describes the result, not the plan.

title: Tables
summary: Named relations: a heading of columns and a body of rows. Duplicates depend on whether you mean bag or set.

title: Primary Keys
summary: A column (or set) that uniquely identifies a row. The handle the rest of the schema points at.

title: Foreign Keys
summary: A column that must match a key in another table. Referential integrity as a constraint, not a hope.

title: Constraints
summary: Declarations the engine enforces: NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK, FK — integrity that survives a bad insert.

title: Joins
summary: Combining rows from two relations by a predicate: inner, left, right, full, cross, and the nested-loop vs hash implementations.

title: Aggregation
summary: GROUP BY, HAVING, and the reduction of many rows to a statistic.

title: Subqueries
summary: A query used as a value, a table, or a predicate. Correlated vs uncorrelated is the performance fork.

title: Indexes
summary: Auxiliary structures (usually B+ trees) that make predicates cheap at the cost of writes and space.

title: Views
summary: Named queries. Virtual by default; materialized when you cache the result.

title: Transactions
summary: A grouping of reads and writes that should succeed or fail as a unit.

title: ACID
summary: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability — the classical transaction contract.

title: Isolation Levels
summary: Read uncommitted through serializable: which anomalies you tolerate for concurrency.

title: Locks (DB)
summary: Shared/exclusive, row/table, intention locks. Two-phase locking as a correctness argument.

title: MVCC
summary: Readers see a snapshot; writers create versions. Postgres and InnoDB's answer to blocking reads.

title: Database Concurrency
summary: Interleaving transactions without losing integrity. Conflict serializability is the theory.

title: Normalization
summary: Decomposing schemas to remove redundancy. Normal forms are tests, not decorations.

title: 1NF
summary: Atomic values in cells; no repeating groups. The floor of the relational model.

title: 2NF
summary: 1NF plus no partial dependence of a non-key attribute on part of a composite key.

title: 3NF
summary: 2NF plus no transitive dependence of a non-key attribute on the key.

title: BCNF
summary: Every determinant is a candidate key. Stricter than 3NF; sometimes you lose a dependency.

title: Query Optimization
summary: Turning SQL into a cheap plan: statistics, join order, and access paths.

title: Query Planners
summary: Cost-based vs rule-based planners, EXPLAIN, and why the optimizer is the real engine.

title: Storage Engines
summary: The physical implementation: heap files, clustered indexes, InnoDB vs MyISAM vs LSM.

title: Buffer Pool
summary: The database's cache of disk pages. Replacement policy, dirty pages, and checkpoints.

title: Write-Ahead Log
summary: Log the change before the page. Redo/undo, crash recovery, and replication's raw feed.

title: B-Trees
summary: Balanced multiway trees. Internal nodes hold keys and children; used widely in filesystems and DBs.

title: B+ Trees
summary: All values in leaves, leaves linked. The index structure behind almost every relational PK.

title: Replication (DB)
summary: Copying data to other nodes: statement vs row, sync vs async, failover.

title: Sharding
summary: Partitioning rows across machines by a key. Hotspots and resharding are the cost.

title: Partitioning
summary: Splitting a table by range, list, or hash — within one instance or across them.

title: Key-Value Stores
summary: The simplest NoSQL: get/put by key. Redis, Dynamo-style systems.

title: Document Stores
summary: JSON/BSON documents with secondary indexes. Schema-on-read, query-on-fields.

title: Column Stores
summary: Values stored by column, not row. Analytics, compression, and vectorized execution.

title: Graph Databases
summary: First-class nodes and edges. Index-free adjacency and graph query languages.

title: Classes
summary: A template for objects: fields, methods, and the invariants that should hold.

title: Objects
summary: A bundle of state and behavior at run time. Identity, state, behavior.

title: Encapsulation
summary: Hiding representation behind an interface so clients do not depend on internals.

title: Abstraction
summary: Showing the essential operations and hiding the rest. Types are the usual vehicle.

title: Inheritance
summary: A subclass reuses and specializes a superclass. Easy to overuse; composition is often healthier.

title: Polymorphism
summary: The same operation, many implementations. Subtype, parametric, and ad-hoc.

title: Interfaces
summary: A named set of operations without a single implementation. The seam for substitution.

title: Composition
summary: Has-a: an object owns or uses another to get work done. Prefer this over deep inheritance.

title: Aggregation
summary: A weaker has-a: parts can outlive the whole. UML's hollow diamond.

title: Association
summary: A structural relationship between objects, with multiplicity and direction.

title: Coupling
summary: How much one module knows about another. High coupling is change contagion.

title: Cohesion
summary: How strongly a module's pieces belong together. High cohesion, low coupling is the cliché because it is true.

title: SOLID
summary: Five design heuristics: SRP, OCP, LSP, ISP, DIP. Tools, not commandments.

title: Factory
summary: A method or object whose job is to create other objects without the caller naming the class.

title: Builder
summary: Stepwise construction of a complex object, often with a fluent interface.

title: Singleton
summary: One instance, globally reachable. Easy to write, hard to test, often a hidden service locator.

title: Adapter
summary: A wrapper that makes an existing interface look like the one a client already knows.

title: Decorator
summary: Add behavior by wrapping, without changing the wrapped object's class.

title: Observer
summary: Subscribers register for events; the subject notifies without knowing who they are.

title: Strategy
summary: A family of interchangeable algorithms behind one interface, chosen at run time.

title: Command
summary: An object that represents a request: execute, undo, queue, log.

title: State Pattern
summary: An object whose behavior changes with an explicit state object, instead of a thick switch.

title: Proxy
summary: A stand-in that controls access: lazy load, remote, access control, virtual.

title: Repository
summary: A collection-like interface over persistent storage, so the domain does not speak SQL.

title: SDLC
summary: The life of software: idea, requirements, design, build, test, deploy, operate, retire.

title: Requirements
summary: What the system must do, and how you will know. Ambiguity here becomes defects later.

title: Software Architecture
summary: The load-bearing decisions: module boundaries, quality attributes, and the trade-offs you will live with.

title: Agile
summary: Short feedback loops, working software, and a willingness to change the plan.

title: Scrum
summary: A particular agile process: sprints, a backlog, a daily, and three roles.

title: Git
summary: A content-addressed snapshot database that happens to be a version control system.

title: GitHub
summary: Hosted Git plus the social layer: PRs, issues, actions, and code review.

title: Version Control
summary: The practice of recording history so you can collaborate, blame, and revert.

title: Code Review
summary: A second brain on the diff: correctness, design, and the shared standard of the codebase.

title: Testing
summary: Executing a program to find discrepancies with an intended spec. Strategy, not just tools.

title: Unit Testing
summary: Fast, isolated tests of a small unit. Mocks are a tool, not the point.

title: Integration Testing
summary: Tests that several components together still honor the contract.

title: End-to-End Testing
summary: Drive the system as a user would. Slow, valuable, and easy to make flaky.

title: CI/CD
summary: Every change is built, tested, and (if you mean it) delivered by a machine.

title: Refactoring
summary: Changing structure without changing behavior, in small safe steps, with tests as the net.

title: Clean Code
summary: Names, size, and structure that make the next change cheaper. Subjective, but not meaningless.

title: Technical Debt
summary: A shortcut that saves now and taxes later. Interest is real; so is overpaying it.

title: Documentation
summary: The artifact that lets a stranger (including future you) use or change the system.

title: Observability
summary: Logs, metrics, traces — enough telemetry to ask new questions of a running system.

title: Browser Architecture
summary: Processes, the rendering engine, the JS engine, and the network stack in one product.

title: DOM
summary: The tree of objects representing a document. JavaScript mutates this; the renderer paints it.

title: CSSOM
summary: The CSS object model: parsed styles as a tree the renderer can query.

title: Rendering
summary: Style, layout, paint, composite. The critical path of a frame, and what makes it jank.

title: JavaScript Engine
summary: Parse, compile (often JIT), optimize, garbage-collect. V8 as the usual example.

title: Event Loop
summary: A queue of tasks and a stack. JavaScript is single-threaded; concurrency is scheduling.

title: Web APIs
summary: The interfaces the browser offers JS: DOM, fetch, storage, workers, observers.

title: Browser Storage
summary: Cookies, localStorage, sessionStorage, IndexedDB — different lifetimes, different threat models.

title: Cookies
summary: Small data the browser stores and sends. HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite are the real topic.

title: HTTP Caching
summary: Freshness, validators, and Cache-Control. The cheapest request is the one you do not make.

title: HTML
summary: The markup language of documents: elements, accessibility tree, and forms.

title: CSS
summary: Selectors, cascade, specificity, layout modes. Visual design as a constraint solver.

title: JavaScript on the Web
summary: Scripts, modules, bundlers, and the rules of the browser as a runtime.

title: TypeScript on the Web
summary: Types that vanish before the network. Tooling is the product.

title: React
summary: UI as a function of state. Reconciliation, hooks, and the cost of renders.

title: Accessibility
summary: Designing so people can perceive and operate the UI. Semantics, keyboard, contrast.

title: Web Performance
summary: Core Web Vitals, payload, main-thread work, and measuring instead of guessing.

title: REST
summary: Resources, representations, and uniform verbs. More than 'JSON over HTTP'.

title: GraphQL
summary: A query language for an application graph. Clients ask for fields; the server resolves them.

title: Web APIs (HTTP)
summary: Designing HTTP APIs: versioning, errors, idempotency, pagination, authn.

title: Authentication
summary: Proving who is calling. Sessions, tokens, and the difference from authorization.

title: Authorization
summary: What an authenticated principal is allowed to do. RBAC, ABAC, and the default deny.

title: JWT
summary: A signed (sometimes encrypted) JSON claim set. Self-contained, revocable only with extra work.

title: OAuth
summary: Delegated authorization. Access tokens, refresh tokens, and PKCE for public clients.

title: Sessions
summary: Server-side (or coordinated) state bound to a client via a cookie or token.

title: WebSockets (Web)
summary: Push from the server without polling. Still TCP, still an origin, still auth.

title: Microservices
summary: Multiple deployable services, aligned to domains, talking over the network. Ops cost included.

title: CIA Triad
summary: Confidentiality, integrity, availability. The three axes every control is arguing about.

title: Authentication (Security)
summary: Verifying identity: something you know, have, are — and why MFA exists.

title: Authorization (Security)
summary: Policy after identity. Confused deputies and over-broad tokens are the usual bugs.

title: Encryption
summary: Making confidentiality a key-management problem. Reversible with the right secret.

title: Hashing
summary: One-way mixing. Integrity checks, password storage (with salt and a KDF), and content addressing.

title: Symmetric Encryption
summary: One key for both directions. AES-GCM as the modern default mode of thought.

title: Asymmetric Encryption
summary: A key pair: encrypt to a public key, or sign with a private key. Slow, so we hybridize.

title: Digital Signatures
summary: Integrity plus authenticity of a message, verifiable with a public key.

title: Certificates
summary: A signed binding of a public key to a name. PKI, CAs, and what browsers actually check.

title: TLS
summary: The protocol under HTTPS: handshake, certificates, AEAD, and forward secrecy.

title: Password Security
summary: Hashing with a slow KDF, unique salts, and never storing reversibly. Phishing is still the breach.

title: SQL Injection
summary: Untrusted input becoming SQL. Parameterized queries are the fix, not filters.

title: XSS
summary: Injecting script into someone else's page. Encode on output; CSP as defense in depth.

title: CSRF
summary: A browser, already authenticated, tricked into a state-changing request. SameSite and tokens.

title: CORS
summary: A browser policy for cross-origin reads. Not an access-control system for your API.

title: OWASP
summary: A map of common web failures. The Top 10 is a syllabus, not a complete threat model.

title: Secure Coding
summary: Defaults that fail closed: validation, least privilege, memory safety, dependency hygiene.

title: Network Security
summary: Segmentation, firewalls, TLS everywhere, and the assumption that the LAN is hostile.

title: Identity Management
summary: Provisioning, SSO, lifecycle, and the directory as the real security boundary.

title: Compiler Design
summary: The architecture of a translator: front end, middle end, back end.

title: Interpreters (Design)
summary: Tree-walk, bytecode VM, or JIT — executing without a native binary.

title: Lexer
summary: The scanner: source characters to tokens, with longest-match and keyword rules.

title: Tokens
summary: The atomic words of a language: identifiers, literals, operators, punctuation.

title: Parser
summary: Tokens to a tree. Recursive descent, Pratt, LR — all enforcing a grammar.

title: AST
summary: An abstract syntax tree: the program as nested structure, comments and punctuation gone.

title: Semantic Analysis
summary: Name resolution, types, definite assignment — the meaning a grammar cannot state.

title: Type Checking
summary: Rejecting programs that would not make sense to execute. Inference vs annotation.

title: Intermediate Representation
summary: A compiler's private language: three-address code, SSA, and why optimization wants it.

title: Optimization
summary: Rewrites that preserve semantics and improve a cost model: inlining, DCE, constant folding.

title: Code Generation
summary: IR to machine code or bytecode: instruction selection, register allocation, calling conventions.

title: Language Runtime
summary: The services compiled code expects: allocator, scheduler, unwinder, class loader.

title: GC (Implementation)
summary: Mark-sweep, copying, generational, concurrent. The mutator/collector contract.

title: Formal Languages
summary: Sets of strings over an alphabet, classified by the machines that recognize them.

title: Regular Expressions
summary: A notation for regular languages. In code they are often more powerful than the theory.

title: DFA
summary: A deterministic finite automaton: one state, one next state, no extra memory.

title: NFA
summary: Nondeterministic finite automata, ε-transitions, and the subset construction to a DFA.

title: Regular Languages
summary: The languages DFAs recognize. Closed under the usual operations; pumping lemma as a weapon.

title: Context-Free Grammars
summary: Productions with a single nonterminal on the left. Programming-language syntax lives here.

title: Pushdown Automata
summary: A finite automaton plus a stack. CFGs and PDAs define the same class.

title: Turing Machines
summary: An infinite tape and a finite control. The standard model of 'computable'.

title: Decidability
summary: A language is decidable if a TM halts on every input with yes or no.

title: Undecidability
summary: Problems no algorithm solves. Reduction is how you prove a new one is in the club.

title: Halting Problem
summary: There is no TM that, given ⟨M, w⟩, decides whether M halts on w.

title: Complexity Theory
summary: Not 'can we compute it' but 'with what resources'. Time and space as functions of n.

title: P
summary: Languages decidable in polynomial time on a deterministic TM. 'Efficient' as a first cut.

title: NP
summary: Languages with polynomial-time verifiable certificates. Not 'non-polynomial'.

title: NP-Hard
summary: At least as hard as every problem in NP, via polynomial-time reductions.

title: NP-Complete
summary: In NP and NP-hard. SAT is the ancestor; Karp's 21 are the family.

title: Distributed Systems
summary: Independent computers that appear, if you are lucky, as one. The network is the computer — and the failure.

title: RPC
summary: Calling a function that happens to run on another machine. Timeouts, retries, and idempotency follow.

title: Message Passing
summary: No shared memory: send and receive. The model of actors, Kafka, and most microservices.

title: Logical Clocks
summary: Ordering events without synchronized wall clocks. Happens-before is the primitive.

title: Lamport Clocks
summary: A counter per process, incremented on events and taking max+1 on receive.

title: Vector Clocks
summary: A timestamp per process so you can tell causality from concurrency.

title: Replication
summary: Several copies of the same state. Leader, quorum, and the conflict that follows a partition.

title: Quorum
summary: R + W > N so reads and writes overlap. The math behind many 'highly available' stores.

title: Consistency Models
summary: Linearizability, sequential, causal, eventual — what a read is allowed to return.

title: Eventual Consistency
summary: If writes stop, replicas converge. Until then, you may see the past.

title: Leader Election
summary: Picking one process to decide. Bully, Raft, and the lease that makes it real.

title: Consensus
summary: Agreeing on a value despite failures. FLP, and why we still run Raft.

title: Raft
summary: A consensus protocol designed to be explainable: leader, log, terms, and majority.

title: Paxos
summary: The classic consensus family. Prepare/accept, and Multi-Paxos as what people actually run.

title: Distributed Transactions
summary: ACID across machines. 2PC is the starting point and often the ending warning.

title: Two-Phase Commit
summary: Prepare then commit. Blocking when the coordinator dies is the textbook cost.

title: Failure Detection
summary: Timeouts, heartbeats, and the fact that you cannot distinguish a slow node from a dead one.

title: Fault Tolerance
summary: Continuing (perhaps degraded) after a failure. Replication, retries, and failover.

title: Network Partitions
summary: The network splits. CAP is the slogan; your timeout is the reality.

title: Distributed Locks
summary: Mutual exclusion across processes. Fencing tokens, and why Redis SET NX is not enough.

title: Scalability
summary: Doing more: vertical until you cannot, then horizontal, with the coordination tax.

title: Availability
summary: The fraction of time a service does useful work. Nines, and the error budget they imply.

title: Reliability
summary: Continuing to be correct under stress. Durability, redundancy, and graceful degradation.

title: Latency
summary: How long an operation takes. Tail latency is the one users feel and p99 is the one you measure.

title: Throughput
summary: Work per unit time. Little's law ties it to latency and concurrency.

title: CAP Theorem
summary: In a partition, you give up linearizability or availability. The rest is engineering.

title: ACID vs BASE
summary: Strict transactions versus an apology-oriented, eventually consistent style.

title: Consistency (Design)
summary: Choosing a consistency model as a product decision, not a database default.

title: Fault Tolerance (Design)
summary: Designing so a dead box is an event, not an outage: redundancy, retries, isolation.

title: Load Balancers
summary: Spread traffic, hide backends, terminate TLS, and health-check the fleet.

title: Reverse Proxies
summary: A server in front of servers: TLS, routing, caching, and a single origin for clients.

title: API Gateways
summary: Auth, rate limits, routing, and protocol translation at the edge of a service fleet.

title: Caches
summary: Remembering expensive results. Aside, through, write-back, and the invalidation problem.

title: Redis
summary: An in-memory data structure server used as cache, lock, queue, and sometimes a database.

title: CDNs
summary: Put bytes closer to users. Edge caches, origin shield, and cache-control as the API.

title: Message Queues
summary: Asynchronous buffers between producers and consumers. Delivery semantics are the design.

title: Kafka
summary: A replicated, partitioned log. Consumers are offsets; retention is a disk, not a RAM, problem.

title: Object Storage
summary: Immutable blobs addressed by key. S3 as the API the industry converged on.

title: Search Engines (Systems)
summary: Crawling, inverted indexes, ranking, and the serving path of a query.

title: Rate Limiters
summary: Token bucket, sliding window, and the distributed counter problem.

title: Consistent Hashing
summary: A ring so that adding a node moves only a 1/n fraction of keys — plus virtual nodes.

title: Circuit Breakers
summary: Stop calling a sick dependency so it can recover — and so you fail fast.

title: Retry and Backoff
summary: Retry is amplification. Jittered exponential backoff and idempotency keys are the adult version.

title: Event-Driven Architecture
summary: Facts emitted as events; consumers decide what to do. Coupling in time is gone; coupling in meaning remains.

title: Microservices (Design)
summary: Independent deploys versus distributed transactions. Draw the seams where the domain already splits.

title: URL Shortener
summary: Tiny unique IDs, 301s, and a write-heavy mapping that must not collide.

title: Twitter / X
summary: Fan-out on write vs read, a home timeline, and the celebrity problem.

title: Chat System
summary: One-to-one and group messages, presence, and delivery at the edge of consistency.

title: Notification System
summary: Fan-out to push, email, SMS, with preferences, retries, and quiet hours.

title: YouTube
summary: Upload, transcode, store, CDN, and a recommendation path that dwarfs the video path.

title: Netflix
summary: Open Connect, adaptive bitrate, and a control plane that is a microservice zoo.

title: Video Streaming
summary: Chunked files, manifests, ABR, and the CDN as the real product.

title: Instagram
summary: Media upload, a graph of follows, and a feed that is part cache, part ranking.

title: WhatsApp
summary: End-to-end encryption, a small server footprint, and queues as the product.

title: Uber
summary: Matching riders to drivers on a map, with dispatch that cannot be a naive query.

title: Ride Sharing
summary: Supply, demand, surge, and location at 1 Hz from millions of phones.

title: Amazon
summary: A catalog, a cart, inventory, and a warehouse network. The original service-oriented giant.

title: Google Search
summary: Crawl, index, rank, and serve in ~100ms. The original warehouse-scale computer.

title: Search Engine
summary: A complete IR pipeline you could sketch: crawler, indexer, query service, ranker.

title: Payment System
summary: Idempotent captures, ledgers, and exactly-once as a business requirement.

title: File Storage
summary: Metadata vs bytes, chunking, dedup, and a namespace that looks like a disk.

title: Food Delivery
summary: Three-sided marketplace: diner, restaurant, courier — with ETAs that lie.

title: Linux Fundamentals
summary: A Unix-like kernel, a userspace, and a culture of small tools composed with pipes.

title: Linux Filesystem
summary: A single tree. Everything is a file — until it is a socket, a namespace, or /proc.

title: Processes (Linux)
summary: fork, exec, wait, and the process tree. pstree is a map of the machine.

title: Threads (Linux)
summary: clone() and NPTL. A thread is a task that shares an address space.

title: Permissions
summary: User, group, other; rwx; and the bits that actually matter: setuid, capabilities, ACLs.

title: Users and Groups
summary: uid, gid, /etc/passwd, and the real vs effective IDs a process carries.

title: Shell
summary: A REPL that launches programs, expands globs, and wires file descriptors.

title: Bash (Unix)
summary: The language of automation on Unix: functions, arrays, set -euo pipefail.

title: Pipes
summary: stdout of one process into stdin of the next. The Unix idea in one character.

title: Redirection
summary: <, >, >>, 2>&1 — the file-descriptor algebra of the shell.

title: Environment Variables
summary: A string map inherited by children. Configuration without a config file.

title: SSH (Ops)
summary: Remote login, keys, agent forwarding, and tunnels you should understand before you use.

title: Signals (Linux)
summary: kill, trap, SIGPIPE, and why a daemon should handle SIGTERM.

title: Networking Commands
summary: ss, ip, ping, traceroute, dig, curl — reading the live network from a box.

title: The /proc Filesystem
summary: A window into the kernel: processes, net, sysctl, and the files that are not on disk.

title: System Calls (Linux)
summary: The actual ABI: unistd, strace, and the handful of calls that implement a Unix.

title: Package Management
summary: apt, dnf, pacman: dependency graphs, signatures, and why you pin in production.

title: Cloud Fundamentals
summary: Someone else's computers, APIs in front of them, billed by the hour or the request.

title: IaaS
summary: VMs, disks, and networks as API objects. You still own the guest OS.

title: PaaS
summary: You bring code; the platform brings the runtime, scaling, and a lot of opinions.

title: SaaS
summary: Software delivered as a service. You are now on the other side of the API.

title: Virtual Machines
summary: A hypervisor multiplexing hardware. Isolation that looks like a computer.

title: Containers
summary: Namespaces + cgroups + a filesystem image. Not a VM, despite the UX.

title: Object Storage (Cloud)
summary: Durable blobs, eleven nines of marketing, and a consistency model you must read.

title: Cloud Networking
summary: VPCs, subnets, security groups, and the fact that 'the network' is now software.

title: IAM
summary: Identities, roles, policies. The blast radius of a leaked key is the whole account.

title: Autoscaling
summary: Add or remove capacity from a metric. Cold starts and flapping are the failure modes.

title: Serverless
summary: You deploy functions; the platform scales to zero. Timeouts, payloads, and vendor glue.

title: Cloud Monitoring
summary: Host metrics, managed-service metrics, and the dashboard that is not a substitute for traces.

title: Cloud Logging
summary: Centralized logs as a billed firehose. Structure them or drown.

title: Docker
summary: Images, containers, and a daemon. The packaging format the cloud standardized on.

title: Kubernetes
summary: A control plane for containers: desired state, reconciliation, and a lot of YAML.

title: Infrastructure as Code
summary: The network and the boxes are in git. Plan, apply, and review like software.

title: Terraform
summary: A graph of resources and a state file. Providers for every cloud, including the ones you regret.

title: Deployment Strategies
summary: Rolling, recreate, blue/green, canary — how you swap the running bits.

title: Blue/Green Deployment
summary: Two environments; flip the pointer. Instant rollback, double the capacity during the cut.

title: Canary Deployment
summary: Send a fraction of traffic to the new version and watch the error budget.

title: Monitoring
summary: Known-unknowns: the dashboards you designed. Alerts that page a human should be rare and true.

title: Logging (SRE)
summary: A debug interface for production. Cardinality, retention, and PII.

title: Metrics
summary: Numbers over time: RED, USE, and the histograms that make percentiles honest.

title: Tracing
summary: A request as a tree of spans across services. Sampling is not optional at scale.

title: SLIs
summary: The measurements that stand in for user happiness: availability, latency, quality.

title: SLOs
summary: A target on an SLI, and an error budget that tells you when to slow down shipping.

title: SLAs
summary: The SLO you wrote into a contract, with money attached.

title: Incident Response
summary: Detect, mitigate, communicate, learn. The runbook is the product.

title: Reliability
summary: SRE as an engineering discipline: toil, error budgets, and making tomorrow quieter.

title: AI Fundamentals
summary: Building machines that act as if they were intelligent: search, knowledge, learning.

title: Search (AI)
summary: State spaces, BFS/DFS/A*, and heuristics. Planning as graph search.

title: Knowledge Representation
summary: Logic, frames, graphs — making facts a machine can query and update.

title: Planning
summary: Choosing a sequence of actions to reach a goal. STRIPS, and why the real world is not STRIPS.

title: Reasoning
summary: Inference over a knowledge base: forward, backward, and the incompleteness you live with.

title: Probabilistic AI
summary: When the world is noisy: Bayes nets, HMMs, and decisions under uncertainty.

title: Supervised Learning
summary: Learn a mapping from labeled examples. Classification and regression are the two headlines.

title: Unsupervised Learning
summary: Structure without labels: clusters, density, and compressed representations.

title: Regression
summary: Predict a continuous target. Linear models, residuals, and regularization.

title: Classification
summary: Predict a discrete label. Decision boundaries, class imbalance, and calibration.

title: Decision Trees
summary: Axis-aligned splits that you can read. Easy to overfit, easy to ensemble.

title: Random Forests
summary: Bagged trees with feature randomness. Strong off-the-shelf tabular models.

title: SVM
summary: Maximum-margin classifiers, kernels, and the dual that made them famous.

title: k-NN
summary: Classify by the labels of the nearest neighbors. The dataset is the model.

title: Clustering
summary: k-means, hierarchical, density-based. There is no single right partition.

title: PCA
summary: Orthogonal directions of variance. A linear compression, not a mystery.

title: Feature Engineering
summary: Turning raw observations into the numbers a model can use. Still half the job.

title: Evaluation
